title: FIGMAS and MAS Standards Initiatives
content: Quantitative analysis requires the use of well-characterized reference materials and standards (RMS) in order to obtain reliable data about the composition of unknown materials. There are many uses for RMS, including instrumental calibration, data quality assurance, comparison of results between different laboratories, and long-term checks on instrumental stability, e.g. [1]. Candidates for RMS should be compositionally homogeneous at the scale of analysis, chemically stable and resistant to degradation over time, easy to mount and polish, and easy to use. RMS should exist in large enough quantities to be readily available to all laboratories, since many techniques require the use of RMS including (but not limited to) those performing energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), wavelength dispersive spectroscopy (WDS), secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS), and X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (XRF). In addition, RMS should have accurate, independently verified compositions that are provided along with the physical material.
